read.sections.0.heading.back: Maps show a place from above
read.sections.0.heading.source: A map shows a place from above

read.sections.0.text.note: Back-translation check: 'kayu' is used for 'sticks' (stick charts) and 'kepingan tanah liat' for 'clay tablet'. Check that these sound natural; 'batang kayu' may be clearer.
read.sections.0.text.back: A map is a drawing of a place, usually as seen by a bird from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the mapmaker chooses what to include. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, and a rain map shows the places with the most rain. Humans have been making maps since thousands of years ago. About 2,500 years ago, someone in the area that is now Iraq made a map of the world on a clay tablet. The map shows the city of Babylon in its centre. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made charts from sticks and seashells. The sticks showed the movement of the sea waves, and the shells showed islands.
read.sections.0.text.source: A map is a drawing of a place, usually as a bird would see it from the sky. A map cannot show everything, so the mapmaker chooses what to include. For example, a bus map shows bus stops, and a rain map shows where it rains most. People have made maps for thousands of years. About 2,500 years ago, someone in today's Iraq made a map of the world on a clay tablet. It shows the city of Babylon in the middle. In the Marshall Islands in the Pacific Ocean, sailors made charts from sticks and shells. The sticks showed how ocean waves moved, and the shells showed islands.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: A map is a picture of a place. A map shows that place from above, the way a bird sees it. A map cannot show all things. The people who make it choose what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People have been making maps since long ago. Someone in the area now called Iraq made a map on clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps with sticks and seashells. The shells showed islands.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: A map is a picture of a place. It shows the place from above, like a bird sees it. A map cannot show everything. The person who makes it picks what to show. A bus map shows bus stops. People made maps long ago too. Someone in what is now Iraq made a map on clay. Sailors in the Marshall Islands made maps with sticks and shells. The shells showed islands.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Four tools help you read a map
read.sections.1.heading.source: Four tools help you read a map

read.sections.1.text.note: Translator: 'Footpath' is 'lorong pejalan kaki' everywhere so it is not confused with the key word 'laluan' (route). Check that it sounds natural. Back-translation check: Translator's flag: 'lorong pejalan kaki' is used for 'footpath' throughout so it is not confused with the key word 'laluan' (route). Check that it sounds natural; 'lorong' can also mean 'alley/lane'. Also check 'mata angin ... hanya anak panah' (the compass rose being just an arrow) and whether 'alat' reads naturally for map parts like title and key.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most maps have four tools that help you read them. The title tells you what the map is about. The key, which is also called the legend, explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, line or shape that stands for something that really exists. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river, and the green square is the community centre. The compass points show direction, and sometimes they are just an arrow pointing north. The scale shows how distance on the map compares with real distance. On this map, one square is 100 metres, so the four-square-long footpath is about 400 metres long.
read.sections.1.text.source: Most maps include four tools that help you read them. The title tells you what the map is about. The key, which is also called a legend, explains each symbol. A symbol is a colour, line or shape that represents something real. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river, and a green square is the community centre. The compass rose shows directions, and sometimes it is simply an arrow pointing north. The scale shows how distance on the map compares with real distance. On this map, one square is 100 metres, so the four-square footpath is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Most maps have four tools. The title tells what the map is about. The key tells the meaning of each symbol. A symbol is a small shape, line or colour. A symbol stands for a real thing. On the Riverstone map, the blue line is the river. The compass points show north, south, east and west. The scale helps you see distance. Here, one square is 100 metres. The path to the centre is four squares. So, its length is about 400 metres.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Most maps have four tools. The title says what the map is about. The key tells what each symbol means. A symbol is a small shape, line or colour. It stands for a real thing. On the Riverstone map, a blue line is the river. The compass rose shows north, south, east and west. The scale helps you see how far things are. Here, one square is 100 metres. The path to the centre is four squares. So it is about 400 metres long.

read.sections.2.text.back: The footpath from East Homes is about 400 metres, but the main road route is about 700 metres, so the footpath is the shorter route. But is it the best route for every visitor? The map does not tell you whether the path is muddy, has steps, or has lights at night. The map also does not show whether the footbridge is open today. People who use the path every day know this information. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence, then asks local residents who know the place. Maps are very useful, but a map is not the place itself.

People who use the path every day know this information. A careful map reader uses the map as evidence and then asks local people who know the place. A map is extremely useful, but it is not the place itself.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Back-translation check: The simpler text says 'lorong yang melalui jambatan' and 'laluan tepi jalan raya' rather than 'jalan utama'. This matches the looser English ('path over the bridge', 'way by the road'), but check that it does not confuse learners.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The path that goes over the bridge is 400 metres. The route beside the road, on the other hand, is 700 metres. So, the path is the shorter route. But is it the best route? The map does not tell us everything. Is the path muddy? Does the path have steps? Is it dark at night? People who walk there every day know. So, look at the map first. Then, ask people who know the place.

watch.summary.back: In this short video, explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes maps of Great Britain. Every Ordnance Survey map has a key, which is also called a legend. The key lists the symbols and states the meaning of each one. A symbol is a small picture, line or colour. A symbol stands for a real thing, such as a path, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show many things in a small area. When you know the symbols, you can understand a place before you go there. Maps from other mapmakers may use different symbols. So, always read the key first.
watch.summary.source: In this short video, the explorer Steve Backshall talks about map symbols. Ordnance Survey makes maps of Great Britain. Every Ordnance Survey map has a key, which is also called a legend. The key lists the symbols and says what each one means. A symbol is a small picture, line or colour. It stands for a real thing, like a path, a river or a building. Symbols save space, so a map can show a lot in a small area. When you know the symbols, you can understand a place before you go there. Maps from other mapmakers may use different symbols. So always read the key first.
